concept.name: Bull steepener
concept.definition: A steepening of the yield curve driven by short-term interest rates falling faster than long-term rates. It is called 'bull' because falling yields mean rising bond prices, and this pattern often appears when the central bank is expected to cut short-term rates.
concept.intuition: The curve steepens from the front end rallying: short rates drop (short bonds rise) faster than long rates.
concept.mechanics: Classified by decomposing the spread change: the 2s10s (or similar) spread widens while the short-end yield falls. A trader positioned for it holds a steepener (long front leg, short back leg), which gains from the widening; the 'bull' label describes the rate-direction component of the move, not a separate instrument.
concept.formula: Condition: Δy_short < 0 and Δ(y_long - y_short) > 0, i.e. the front-end yield falls while the spread widens.
concept.failure_modes: The taxonomy is descriptive, not predictive: labeling a move a bull steepener after the fact does not indicate it will continue. Expectations of rate cuts can already be priced in, so the steepening may be exhausted by the time it is identified; a hawkish surprise can reverse it abruptly.
concept.misconceptions: Bull steepener does not mean all yields rise or that long bonds lose money — typically the whole curve rallies, just more at the front. It is also not inherently bullish for stocks in all environments; a steepener driven by recession panic can coincide with equity selloffs.
concept.example: The 2-year Treasury yield falls from 4.8% to 4.2% on expected Fed cuts while the 10-year falls only from 4.4% to 4.3%; the 2s10s spread widens from -40 bp to +10 bp — a bull steepener.

citations.source: LearnBonds: Bull Flattener, Bear Flattener, Bull Steepener and Bear Steepener Explained
